newsitem.title: USA: Broaddus sees some signs U.S. economy slowing.
newsitem.headline: Broaddus sees some signs U.S. economy slowing.

text.p: Richmond Federal Reserve President Alfred Broaddus said Tuesday that he saw some signs of the economy slowing.
"There have been some signs of slowing as we've moved into the third quarter, tentative signs that demand may be softening," he told a National Economists Club luncheon.
Broaddus pointed in particular to softening retail sales and slowing jobs growth.
Broaddus called the September employment report "weak" though he noted that the jobless rate at 5.2 percent was still "quite low."
"The labor market is...exceptionally tight across the country," he said.
He described recent inflation as "quite modest" and said the economy, in its sixth year of expansion, could only be described in "pretty favorable terms."
"The bottom line on the current situation, as I see it - low unemployment, relatively low inflation, at least for now," he said.
Broaddus said the United States had made a great deal of progress in the fight against inflation. But he added, "we still have some distance to go."
Some Brookings Institute economists have argued that the the U.S. would have more to lose than gain from a drive to achieve stable prices.
Broaddus called their work "a serious paper" but said some analysts have suggested that the conclusions may be sweeping given the limited time frame looked at.

He made clear that he felt price stability would be good for the economy and suggested the Fed may need a more concrete goal for eradicating inflation in order to increase the central bank's credibility.
The Richmond Fed's area was growing strongly, Broaddus said. He pointed out that labor markets in the region were "quite tight," and especially tight in North Carolina.
The Fifth Federal Reserve District, represented by the Richmond Fed, includes Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, the District of Columbia and much of West Virginia.
Asked whether there was evidence that businesses were passing along price increases to consumers, Broaddus said there was no sign of that yet.
"Although there's been some perceived upward movement in wages, we are not seeing evidence that that is being passed on to prices in any general way," he said.

Broaddus said he did not know what jobless rate would constitute full employment, or the non-accelerating inflationary rate of uenmployment (NAIRU). But he cautioned against concluding that it had fallen sharply.

"I don't know where the NAIRU is," he said. "I don't know whether it's come down. I certainly wouldn't want to conclude that it's come down significantly from estimates of a year ago of somewhere in the neighborhood of 5-3/4 to six percent."
